Ecuador Construction Materials Workers Strike Disrupts Supply Chain

A nationwide strike by construction materials workers in Ecuador has entered its fourth day, significantly disrupting the sector’s supply chain and raising concerns among industry stakeholders. The walkout began Monday, with members of the National Union of Materials Workers (Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores de Materiales, SNTM) demanding improved wages, safer working conditions, and enhanced health benefits across cement, aggregate, and concrete production plants.

Production at several major manufacturers, including Andina Cementos and Constructores Unidos, has reportedly slowed or halted entirely. According to the Ecuadorian Association of Construction Materials Producers (AECOM), the stoppage is impacting roughly 70% of national output, with daily losses estimated at $2.5 million.

“We are facing an unprecedented situation,” stated AECOM president Luis Fernando Robles. “If a resolution is not achieved soon, the backlog could take months to clear, affecting supply commitments well into the third quarter.”

Truck convoys at major production sites in Guayaquil and Quito remain idle, as workers maintain picket lines at plant entrances. SNTM Secretary-General Patricia Valverde asserted, “Our members are essential to the country’s development, and we will not return to work until our demands are addressed at the negotiating table.”

Industry analysts warn that extended disruption could lead to shortages of cement, aggregates, and ready-mix concrete, potentially delaying ongoing projects. “The immediate effect is a reduction in deliveries to distributors and construction sites,” said local industry analyst Mario Cisneros. “Inventories are declining rapidly, especially in high-demand urban centers.”

The Ministry of Labor has called for renewed negotiations, but talks have so far failed to yield an agreement. As the strike continues, sector participants are closely monitoring developments, with many expressing concern over the potential for long-term market volatility and increased materials prices.
